The patched sources and models are those sources with the patch applied, so nothing is copied or patched. A stale page leads with a warning naming what changed; the router's verdict cell says (⚠ stale), index.json records snapshot, and --render-only prints NNN-name: stale (why). Rendering rewrites no result. 'Why the verdict is right' holds the author's explanation only when the run gave the expected result; otherwise the section is 'What the example expected', naming both results and quoting the explanation as the expected one's.

Every page moved by one line under Evidence: all 140 recorded results predate claims, so they render as unknown. No recorded result misses its expectation, so no explanation section moved. A full --render-only takes 2.6 s. Verified: test_build.py 115 tests (new SnapshotTest: current, stale by patch, scope, statement, sources with build output left out, and claim format; evidence not the bundle; unknown; --render-only showing a stale fixture in the page, router row and index.json without rewriting the result; the explanation for missed, unevaluable and older results), test_pipeline.py 20 tests.

commits.summary: build.py: every command is a logged stage, and a pipeline job keeps each attempt's workspace (verification pending)
commits.body:
Step 3d of llm-dlc/loops/build-orchestration.md, which completes Phase 3. Every command build.py makes goes through stage(name, command). Inside an attempt, its stdout and stderr stream into logs/NN-name.stdout/.stderr as it runs, and logs/stages.jsonl gets a line as each stage starts and ends. A path-free progress line is printed for each, and the attempt records stages (name, exited/killed/timed-out/not-started, exit code, seconds, log paths). A timeout raises with the output so far. In a pipeline job the scratch directory sits under $VERIFY_WORKDIR/.build-py and is never removed, so each attempt keeps its patched copy (harnesses, the tools' work directories), logs and evidence, named by attempt.workspace; the pipeline keeps that work directory for a job that does not pass and collects only declared outputs. Outside the pipeline each copy is removed when its run ends, as before. The unpatched baseline of a regression proof no longer compiles tests.

Measured first: an app copies in 0.01-0.05 s and compiles main in 0.56-0.73 s and tests in 0.56-0.72 s (Quorum, Crosscut, Mica), so a cross-job baseline cache would save under a second per job and is not added; Box Office's Gradle builds will be timed by attempt.stages from the jobs below. Checked and not needed: git apply inside a repository's tree patches the copy as in /tmp, since it prefixes the patch's paths with its directory; a test covers it. Verified: test_build.py 123 tests (new StagesTest: streamed logs and records, check, a timeout keeping partial output, a killed stage, capture outside an attempt, an interrupted run leaving claim.json, the copy and every stage's log in the kept workspace, a pipeline attempt's stages and workspace, the copy removed outside the pipeline, the baseline compiled without tests), test_pipeline.py 20 tests, no page moved under --render-only.

commits.summary: Loop brief sound-verdicts.md: named gaps, results that state their assumptions, and agent-advised contracts
commits.body:
A new feature-loop brief, llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md, approved by the user on 2026-11-05. Its inputs are two outside reviews of the repository at c4fa2f64, kept beside it: sound-verdicts-review-ecosystem.md (jvmcontract against JBMC, KeY, OpenJML, JPF, SAW, ByteBack, VeriFast, Dafny and proof checkers) and sound-verdicts-review-jbmc.md (where investing in CBMC/JBMC would pay). Both put first that the native engine approximates some Java it doesn't implement instead of refusing it, so a false claim can come back Verified; that was checked at HEAD (opaque JDK constructor and method fallbacks, monitors without a null check, fields keyed by name, three interval stages always, JBMC read as text).

The plan: Phase 1 names every unimplemented construct as a gap, with strict (refuse), assume (today's approximation, recorded) and advised modes, strict being the library's default, a static scan measuring the coverage cost first, identity and initialization fixes, a conformance corpus checked against a real JVM, and an opt-in JBMC confirmation. Phase 2 makes the result state its domain, assumptions, observations, bounds, models, solver and vacuity as data. Phase 3 is the advised mode: the run hands the driving agent its open gaps, the agent proposes contracts, and the tool proves them against JDK bytecode, tests them on a real JVM, or records them as trusted, with a contract library and a CI trust limit; the library never calls an LLM itself. Phase 4 is JBMC adapter work without a fork, Phase 5 measurement. The user settled the open questions: strict by default without re-running the recorded examples in strict mode yet (they run in assume until decided), and this loop before build-orchestration.md's deferred phases, which its Progress now notes.

The JBMC patch queue, the earlier draft's last phase, is split into llm-dlc/loops/jbmc-patch-queue.md, a working draft with no loop settings, to refine over time.

commits.summary: Gap scan: jvmcontract gaps names what the tool's own checker approximates, and every B9/B11 example records what strict mode would cost it
commits.body:
Step 1a of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. lib/src/bmc/gaps.rs walks the bytecode a proof's roots may reach, resolving calls as the engine does, and names each construct the engine approximates rather than implements as a gap with a stable id (kind and member, @jdk-<version> for a JDK call): a skipped JDK constructor, a void or reference-returning JDK instance method, a monitor (no null check), a field hidden by a subclass, a literal compared by reference, a class initializer the engine never runs, an object converted inside a string concatenation. It also lists the JDK calls the engine reproduces exactly and relies on, and what it already refuses. The new command is `jvmcontract gaps --classes DIR --target C#m [--json]`. bmc::models_jdk_static gives the scan the engine's list of modelled static JDK methods. `build.py --scan-gaps` compiles each B9/B11 example on a javac app, scans both versions of a regression proof, and replaces the example's 'Gap scan (...)' note.

Result over the 56 examples scanned: strict mode moves no recorded verdict. 54 meet no gap. 013 and 071 (Quorum's vote rule, proved by JBMC) meet four enum class initializers and a literal compared by reference, but the native engine already refuses both, since enum constants are static fields that aren't compile-time constants. Not scanned: Box Office's 006-008 (its Gradle verifier), the real-world 105-109 (no classes in the repository), and the approaches that are not proofs over bytecode.

Correction to the brief: step 1b's allow-list of exact JDK calls ('Object.<init>, and calls already covered by lib/models') is too narrow. The scan shows 14 examples relying on Record.<init>() and 25 on the JDK exceptions' (), (String) and (String, Throwable) constructors. These change nothing a proof observes and throw nothing, so they belong on the list; gaps::exact_jdk_call is that list. Also, the string-conversion gap only arises in bytecode from javac 9-18: from JDK 19, javac calls String.valueOf first, which the engine refuses.

Verified with a new integration test (both review reproducers, a void JDK mutator of an argument array via Random.nextBytes, field hiding, literal identity, a class initializer and the exact calls, each by id) and GapScanTest in test_build.py (133 tests). The full lib suite passes (118 unit, 51 integration tests). `build.py --render-only` reports no page stale; the notes are not part of any claim.

commits.summary: Gaps as data: the tool's own checker refuses a JDK call it does not implement by name under --gaps strict, or names it as an assumption under --gaps assume
commits.body:
Step 1b of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. The native engine (lib/src/bmc) used to approximate a JDK constructor (skipped), a void JDK instance method (did nothing) and a reference-returning one (a fresh object), so a claim the JVM refutes could come back Verified: new ArrayList<>(n) throws for a negative n, Random.nextBytes fills its argument array. These are now gaps the engine meets as it runs, by the same stable ids and classification as the 1a scan (gaps::jdk_instance_call), with the string conversion of an object in an indy concatenation. Under --gaps strict, the library's default, the path ends at the gap; a run that met one is Unverifiable unless another path is a violation, and its reason lists every gap met with its sites. Under --gaps assume the old approximation stays, and the verdict says so: '✓ ..., assuming 1 behaviour the tool's own checker does not implement (--gaps assume)', with an 'assumed:' line per gap and the gaps in the JSON outcome's search (gap_mode, gaps: id, kind, call, sites, approximation, refused/assumed). monitorenter/monitorexit now throw NullPointerException on null and otherwise do nothing, so synchronized (null) is a violation in both modes, and the scan no longer reports monitors. --engine auto doesn't hand a refused gap to JBMC, which approximates a call it has no bytecode for without naming it (step 4c). The engine's module docs have a table of every instruction and call as implemented, modelled, a gap or refused. A unit test decodes every opcode and checks it has a row there, and that every gap kind has one in gaps.rs.

build.py passes --gaps only where the own checker decides the verdict (engine native or auto). The mode is the example's approach.gaps (new in the schema), or 'assume' for a recorded example (RECORDED_GAP_MODE), so a rerun records assumptions rather than changing a verdict. result.search keeps gapMode and gaps, and a verified label and page name each assumed gap. Docs: lib/README.md, examples/README.md, the verify-bytecode skill's reference.

Verified: cargo test --release passes (119 unit, 52 integration). The new integration test proves both review reproducers and a void mutator of an argument array on the native engine and under --engine auto in both modes. It also runs them on a real JVM (IllegalArgumentException, NullPointerException, an array changed), and runs a regression proof with a JDK constructor added. The 136 build.py tests pass, and --render-only changed no page: no recorded result has a gap (1a), so no pipeline job was needed.

Where the brief is out of date: 1b's 'implemented, modelled, or a gap' needs a fourth class, refused, which is most of what the engine doesn't handle and stays a refusal with a reason. Its allow-list is wider than 'Object.<init> and lib/models': Record.<init> and the JDK exceptions' (), (String) and (String, Throwable) constructors, as 1a found. The checked-at-HEAD list's monitor item is now fixed. Hidden fields, literal identity and class initializers are still approximated silently in both modes until 1c. The gap mode is recorded as an attempt option, not as part of the claim, so recorded claims don't go stale; 2a's statement should take it in.

commits.summary: Identity and initialization: a hidden field is a second field and a literal one object, as on the JVM, and a class initializer the tool's own checker does not run is a named gap
commits.body:
Step 1c of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. Fields are now resolved by the JVM's field lookup (JVMS 5.4.3.2, ClassPath::resolve_field). A field that a subclass declares again is kept as a second field under its declaring class's name (ClassPath::field_key), in both the tool's own checker and the interpreter that replays its witnesses. The interpreter had the same name-only keying, so it confirmed the engine's wrong witness. Each path of the checker keeps one object per distinct string or class literal, as the JVM interns them. A string concatenation stays a new object, as JLS 15.18.1 says; this was checked on JDK 25.

A class whose initialization runs an application <clinit> is a class-initializer gap. gaps::initializers lists those initializers in JVMS 5.5 order: superclasses first, then superinterfaces with default methods, then the class itself. The engine meets the gap at a path's first new, getstatic or invokestatic of the class, and the static scan uses the same function. Under --gaps strict the path is refused by name; under --gaps assume the initializer is taken to have run and thrown nothing, and the verdict names it. --engine auto now asks JBMC when every gap the checker refused is a class initializer, because JBMC runs initializers; JDK-call gaps still don't fall back. Because hidden fields and literal identity are now implemented, they are no longer gap kinds (the result schema and docs follow).

Verified by the new integration test identity_and_initialization_agree_with_the_jvm, which runs every claim on a real JVM first. On the parent commit's binary, four claims the JVM refutes came back Verified: hiding 'result == 2', sameLiteral '!result', sameClass '!result', and boom 'result == n', which throws ExceptionInInitializerError on the JVM. Now the first three are violations that the interpreter replays. boom is refused by name under strict and Verified-with-assumption under assume, and JBMC gives a violation (ExceptionInInitializerError) for it under auto; a harmless initializer is refused under strict too. cargo test --release passes (119 unit, 53 integration tests), and so do build.py's 136 tests. build.py --scan-gaps rescanned all 56 B9/B11 examples in 41 s. Only 013's and 071's notes changed (their literal-identity gap is gone, their four enum initializers stay), so strict mode still moves no recorded verdict and no verification job is needed.

Where the brief is out of date: its 'checked at HEAD' list still says fields are keyed by name, and the 1a Progress entry lists hidden-field and literal-identity as kinds. Both are now historical. 1c allowed 'reference comparison on a literal is a gap'; the faithful identity was implemented instead. 1b's rule that auto never falls back after a refused gap is now limited to gaps JBMC also approximates. Still refused: a getstatic of a String constant field, which javac inlines as ldc anyway. Next: 1d, the conformance corpus.

commits.summary: Conformance corpus: 93 claims about 54 small methods, each held to a real JVM, and no Verified the JVM refutes from the tool's own checker under strict (verification pending)
commits.body:
Step 1d of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. lib/tests/conformance.rs runs a corpus of small Java methods (lib/tests/conformance/conformance/Conformance.java). The cases cover the gap reproducers of steps 1b and 1c, JDK constructors given a negative capacity, exceptions (finally over a return, nested handlers, bounds, casts, throw null, rethrow), aliasing, null arrays, record constructors, dispatch, and arithmetic edge cases (MIN_VALUE / -1 in both widths, negative remainders, shift counts of 32, 33, 64 and -1, narrowing, overflow). The JVM is the reference. A Java runner (lib/tests/conformance/Runner.java) runs every call, and every claim's generated property harness, each in a class loader of its own. So whether a claim is refuted is the JVM's answer on the harness, and every witness an engine reports is run on the JVM as well.

Inline, in 11 s, the corpus checks the tool's own checker under --gaps strict and assume, and the interpreter against the JVM call by call. Of the 93 claims, 48 are refuted on the JVM. None of them is Verified under strict, and every violation's witness refutes the harness on the JVM. Under assume a refuted claim is Verified only with its gap named. The native verdict is recorded for each claim, so coverage changes show up too.

The corpus found a bug in the interpreter, which replays every witness and executes the behavioural contracts (B8). new ArrayList<>(n), new HashMap<>(n), new HashSet<>(n), new HashMap<>(4, f) and new StringBuilder(n) returned normally there for a negative capacity (or a load factor of 0 or less), where the JVM throws IllegalArgumentException or NegativeArraySizeException. The test failed on capacity(-1) before the fix, which makes lib/src/interp/natives.rs throw what the JVM does. This is the brief's point that the engines and the interpreter share semantics, so their agreement proves nothing about the JVM.

A null array parameter, or one array passed as two parameters, is outside the domain both engines prove over (JBMC runs under --java-assume-inputs-non-null), but the domain line did not say so. It now reads 'a: int[] of length ≤ 8, not null', ending '; no two the same array' when there are two arrays or more (harness::domain, used by both regression and property proofs). The corpus has three such cases, and checks that a Verified for them states the restriction that leaves out the JVM's refuting input. Pages already recorded keep the old text until they are re-run; build.py's domain regexes still match.

The brief is out of date in one respect: it plans the JBMC side of the corpus as examples under a new false-success defect tag. A corpus is a table of claims over one class, and examples would put one claim on each page. So JBMC and --engine auto run the same corpus in an ignored test, the_corpus_agrees_with_the_jvm_under_jbmc_and_auto (cargo test --release --test conformance -- --ignored), queued as pipeline job 20261106-021741-conformance-corpus-under-jbmc-and-engine. The tag is not added. lib/README.md documents the corpus and the domain's wording.

commits.summary: Confirming mode: --engine auto --confirm has JBMC prove again what the tool's own checker proved, and a disagreement is no verdict of either (verification pending)
commits.body:
Step 1e of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. Under --engine auto --confirm, for property and regression proofs, a statement the own checker proved goes to JBMC, which proves it again in one run over every input. That run uses the same harness and class path; the interval stages only find small witnesses sooner. The result's search.confirmation has a status (confirmed, disagreed, no-verdict, not-asked), the checker, its seconds and a reason, and a line under the ✓ says it in words. JBMC refuting the proof gives Unverifiable, 'the engines disagree' (finding engines-disagree), with JBMC's witness as the counterexample. The interpreter's run of the harness on that witness is shown but decides nothing, since it shares the own checker's models. A proof that assumed a JDK call under --gaps assume is not sent to JBMC, which would approximate the same call without naming it. An assumed class initializer is checked, since JBMC runs it. The option is opt-in, and the CLI refuses it under any engine but auto.

Departures from the brief: it says a disagreement is 'its own outcome, never either verdict'. Here that is Unverifiable plus the disagreed status, not a fourth Verdict, because every caller already treats Unverifiable as no verdict. A JBMC run with no verdict leaves the own checker's proof standing (exit 0), with the result saying it is not confirmed. build.py does not pass --confirm, so no recorded result changes. Seen, not fixed: a relative --jbmc path fails, because JBMC runs in the work directory.

Verified: confirm_reports_what_jbmc_made_of_a_proof_of_the_own_checker (lib/tests/conformance.rs) uses a script standing in for JBMC, since JBMC is not run inline. It covers each status, both drivers, the single full-range command line, the JSON and the CLI refusal. The conformance corpus's native test still passes. cargo test --release: 119 unit tests and the conformance tests pass. The 53 integration tests passed on a second run in 55 s. On the first run, 625 s on a loaded machine, the own checker's regression proof of the Pricing rounding refactor (integration.rs:1391) did not come back a violation; the test passes alone in 17 s and in the full rerun, and --confirm is off there. The search's time-dependent budgets are the likely cause, so it is worth watching. Clippy is clean on the changed files.

The real JBMC runs the whole corpus under auto --confirm, strict and assume, in the new ignored test the_corpus_agrees_with_the_jvm_under_auto_confirm: pipeline job 20261106-024336-conformance-corpus-under-engine-auto-con. Phase 1 is complete apart from that job and 20261106-021741. Next: 2a, the statement as data.

commits.summary: The statement as data: every verdict of a regression or property proof carries what it is about, its domain, assumptions with their basis, observations, bounds, models, checker, gap mode and confirmation, and the page states it (verification pending)
commits.body:
Step 2a of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. A proof line could read the same for two verdicts about different statements. Now jvmcontract's equivalence and prove outcomes carry 'stated' (lib/src/statement.rs) whenever a harness was built, whatever the verdict. It covers the domain D: each parameter's kind (primitive, array, or record with its components), whether null is among its values, an array's longest length, and whether two arrays may be one (never today). It covers the assumptions A, each with a kind and a basis: stated by the claim (--unchanged-unless, --assume), made by the harness (inputs a record's constructor rejects, or on which --before-arguments throws, are skipped), the checker's engine semantics (the own checker takes every JDK class as initialized; JBMC stubs a JDK method it has no bytecode for), or a gap assumed under --gaps assume, with its id. It covers the observations: what is compared of the result and of an exception (its class among the harness's 15, not its message), and which arrays are compared after the call. Then come the unwinding and array bounds, whether the search was complete, the model bundle's sha256 digest (a SHA-256 written out in lib/src/digest.rs, since the build has no network) with the JDK's version, the checker with its SAT solver (the own checker's bundled CaDiCaL 1.9.5) and any fallback, the gap mode, and the --confirm status.

build.py records it as result.stated (camelCase, kept in format 2's evidence; a B11 property keeps its own). The result schema defines it as $defs/statement. A page states it in one paragraph, 'What the verdict is about', after the proof line. No recorded result has it until it is re-run, so --render-only of every example changed no page. Jobs 20261106-025930-example-144-b9-re-run-its-result-records and 20261106-025930-example-145-b9-re-run-its-result-records re-run the pair that differs only in the array bound (8, where the proof is vacuous, and 12), so two real pages show it. lib/README.md and the verify-bytecode skill's reference describe the field.

Verified inline. The new conformance test the_statement_says_what_a_verdict_is_about runs the own checker on pairs of claims that differ only in the domain (array bound 8 or 4), the observations, an assumption, or the models (on or off), and finds each pair's statements different in that part alone. It also covers a regression proof's two unaliased arrays, scope and result relation, and identical bytecode (checker none). The new StatementTest in test_build.py renders pairs that differ in the domain, observations, assumptions, models or confirmation, and checks that each paragraph says the difference in the sentence about it, and that the recorded field validates against the schema. cargo test --release: 122 unit, 3 conformance (2 ignored, pipeline jobs), 53 integration, all pass. test_build.py: 140 pass. Clippy is clean on the changed files.

Where this departs from the brief: the console report doesn't print the statement (--json and the page do). The search record keeps its own copies of the bounds and gap mode so as not to break its readers. JBMC's solver is recorded as the one asked for (cadical), without the version JBMC bundles. Vacuity is left as it was, for 2b.

commits.summary: Vacuity as a status: a verified regression or property proof says whether it is about any input, non-vacuous (with the probe's witness), vacuous or unknown, and a proof over records says the constructors' agreement is another obligation (verification pending)
commits.body:
Step 2b of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. Every Verified statement now carries stated.vacuity (lib/src/statement.rs, Vacuity): a status of non-vacuous, vacuous or unknown, the basis it is known on, a sentence, and an input that reaches the calls when one was found. Nothing skipping an input before the calls is non-vacuous by the harness. A scope, a precondition, a record built through its constructor or --before-arguments is probed as before (the harness with the calls replaced by a failure, run by the tool's own checker): its violation is now kept as the witness ('not vacuous: span(this=Range[lo=20, hi=20]) reaches the calls'), its proof is vacuous, and no verdict is unknown ('vacuity unknown: ...', where a note nobody read used to be). Identical bytecode is non-vacuous by being identical. Only a Verified has a status, and the exit code stays 0 for a vacuous or unknown one (open question 1). Outcome.vacuous keeps its reason for its existing readers.

The record-constructor caveat the ecosystem review asks for is stated wherever it applies: a 'constructors: ...' line under the verdict, the constructible assumption of the statement, and the page's paragraph, saying that the proof is about the records both versions' constructors accept and whether they accept the same inputs is not part of it. Identical bytecode drops it, since the constructors are among what is identical. build.py ends the page's 'What the verdict is about' paragraph with the vacuity sentence, and a verified label gains ', non-vacuity unknown' (or 'for k of n' properties) where the probe gave no verdict; whether a result matches its example is unchanged, so unknown is not called vacuous. A gap with no contract makes the verdict unverifiable, with the finding gaps-need-contracts and no search. The outcome's advice (--json) holds the claim in words, the JDK version, and for each gap: its stable id, the call with owner, name, descriptor, parameters, result type and sites, what --gaps assume would take it to do, and must_state, the parts a contract must state for its kind (result, exceptions, receiver, arguments, an initializer's static state, purity), each with a question. The template is the draft of step 3b's format: a block per gap id with prove's keys call:, assume:, throws: X when c, assert:, modifies:, written-by:. With no gap, advised is strict, so a gap the scan missed is still refused. Under --engine jbmc, advised is an error, since JBMC's stubs are step 4c's gaps. Unlike strict, which ends a path at its first gap, the scan names every gap the harness reaches.

An initializer whose contract throws nothing and modifies nothing is taken to have run. A contract the engine cannot apply (a TODO left, a call that does not match the id, this or an object parameter in a condition, result != null alone, an initializer that throws or sets state, \old, a string conversion, another JDK's version) is refused with the reason in a note line and in the gap's advice, and its gap stays open; the advice lists the gaps contracts closed, and its template only those still open.

Its format comes from CBMC 6.11.0's own source (report_util.cpp, json_goto_trace.cpp, json_expr.cpp, ui_message.cpp at tag cbmc-6.11.0), since JBMC is not run inline to find it out. It reads the array of messages, property results with the failed property's trace, and the overall cProverStatus. It reads element by element, so a cut-off run or text around the array does no harm. A counterexample's inputs come from the trace's input steps by slot, an array's elements from the assignments before its input, and every value from its bits (signed unless char or boolean; IEEE 754 at width 32 or 64), not from how Java prints it. Only success, with every property SUCCESS or UNREACHABLE, is a proof.

Every result and every run in search.runs now has an ending: verified, counterexample, unwinding-failure, other-failure, timeout, memory-exhausted, killed, solver-failure, unsupported-input, unavailable, unreadable, or the own checker's no-verdict. JbmcResult::out_of_time reads it in place of 4a's text match. The text parser stays as JVMCONTRACT_JBMC_READ=text. JVMCONTRACT_JBMC_READ=both runs JBMC both ways, decides by the JSON, and writes what each reading made of each run to <log>.differential.json (and to the file JVMCONTRACT_JBMC_DIFFERENTIAL names). The schema, lib/README.md and the skill's reference.md describe it.

Verified inline. The integration suite runs the real JBMC 6.11.0 (151 runs, every witness replayed by the interpreter), and it now goes through the JSON reader. A new integration test, the_json_and_the_text_reading_of_jbmc_agree, runs the CLI under both on a proof, counterexamples over an int[] and a long, and an unwinding failure, and every pair of readings agrees. New unit tests cover every ending from fixtures in CBMC's shape, plus the canonical value forms and the differential on stand-ins. The conformance stand-ins answer in JSON when --json-ui is passed. All Rust tests (136 unit, 5 conformance, 58 integration, 1 skill) and the 156 Python tests pass. Re-rendering every page changed none.

Job 20261106-073804-jbmc-read-through-json-ui-agrees-with-th is the brief's differential test. It runs build.py on a copy of examples/ over the 41 recorded B9/B11 JBMC examples under JVMCONTRACT_JBMC_READ=both, and fails on a disagreement or a verdict that moved. The text parser is removed once it passes. Next: 4c, JBMC's stubs as gaps.

commits.summary: JBMC's own approximations are gaps under strict and assume: its stubs of methods it has no bytecode for, the invokedynamic call sites it gives the value zero or null, and the monitors it drops are named from its goto program, and a JBMC proof that reaches one is no verdict under strict (verification pending)

Step 4c, first part, of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. Before JBMC's proof, jvmcontract now runs JBMC with --show-goto-functions on the harness (lib/src/jbmc_gaps.rs). That converts what the proof would and solves nothing: 40 ms on the review's reproducers. It then walks JBMC's own call graph from the harness. Three things count as approximations:
- a method reached with no bytecode on JBMC's class path: JBMC's stub returns any value of its type and does nothing else;
- an invokedynamic that JBMC links to no class of its own making: JBMC takes its value to be zero or null. This covers string concatenation, a record's equals/hashCode/toString, and a lambda for a JDK interface. JBMC never checks the bootstrap method's name, as read from CBMC 6.11.0's lambda_synthesis.cpp;
- a method that synchronizes: JBMC drops monitor instructions, so synchronized (null) throws nothing.
They are gaps with the own checker's ids where the call is the same, plus three JBMC-only kinds: missing-body, invokedynamic and monitor. Stubs that only a JDK class's initializer reaches stay under the statement's engine assumption.

Under --gaps strict (the library's default), a JBMC proof that reaches a gap is Unverifiable, and a counterexample stands only if the interpreter replays it. Under --gaps assume the verdict names each gap. --confirm holds JBMC's proof to its gaps too. build.py now passes the recorded gap mode (assume) to the examples JBMC proves.

Verified inline on the real JBMC 6.11.0 by the new integration test jbmc_own_approximations_are_gaps_in_the_same_modes. JBMC alone proved five claims the JVM refutes: new ArrayList<>(n) returning, Random.nextBytes leaving its array, synchronized (null) returning, a string concatenation being null, and a record unequal to its copy. Under strict all five are now refused by name, and under assume each is Verified naming its gap. A regression proof under --engine jbmc behaves the same. All Rust tests pass (138 unit, 5 conformance, 59 integration, 1 skill), and so do the 157 Python tests. The existing integration tests, with their 151 real JBMC runs, pass unchanged under the new strict default. Re-rendering every page changed none.

Job 20261106-082917-jbmc-s-own-approximations-as-gaps-every runs build.py on a copy of the 41 recorded JBMC examples under assume, where no verdict should move. It tabulates the JBMC gaps each one reaches, which is what strict would cost them.

Where the brief is wrong or out of date:
- It names stubs and the invokedynamic fallback, but not monitors, which JBMC also drops.
- Its acceptance, 1b's reproducers giving the same answer under JBMC in each mode, cannot hold for synchronized (null). JBMC gives a named gap where the own checker gives the violation, which still meets 1b's own acceptance (a named gap or a correct violation).
- Advised gives the same answer only through the own checker, since JBMC does not apply contracts yet. That is 4c's second part, recorded under Progress as next.

commits.summary: JBMC applies the contracts for its gaps: under --engine jbmc --gaps advised a JDK call JBMC stubs takes the contract the own checker would, its call sites rewritten into calls of the contract's method, and a gap with no contract stops the run with the advice

Step 4c, second part, of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md (lib/src/jbmc_contracts.rs). The gaps JBMC's goto-program preflight finds are the advice protocol's scan: a JDK-call gap with no contract stops the run before solving (advice.checker "jbmc"), and contracts are read and checked as for the own checker (proved, tested on a JVM, trusted, the library's records, --max-trust); a JBMC gap has the own checker's id, so one contract serves both checkers. Monitors, unlinked invokedynamic and missing bodies outside the JDK take no contract: the advice lists them as approximated by JBMC whatever the contracts, and the proof is refused as under strict. JBMC runs the same GapContracts class: every call site of a closed gap in the harness and application class directories is rewritten into an invokestatic of the contract's method (shared::redirect_calls now takes any call kind; invokeinterface becomes invokestatic plus two nops, so no offset moves), a constructor through GapContractCalls.k<N>, which takes the uninitialized receiver; the intrinsics are a class over org.cprover.CProver (nondetInt/nondetLong, assume(false), a nondet loop over an array's elements, and open as an AssertionError that JBMC reports as its own property, which is no verdict: an input outside the contract's assume:). A second preflight on the rewritten class path holds whatever JBMC still approximates. A call site whose JDK method an application class overrides, calls from JDK bytecode and jars are not rewritten, so their gaps stay open. Under auto, JBMC's turn applies the own checker's contracts. The verdict reads 'relying on N contracts for gaps of JBMC'; build.py and the schema (advice.checker) name JBMC on the page. Both drivers no longer refuse --gaps advised under --engine jbmc.

Verified inline on the real JBMC 6.11.0 by jbmc_applies_the_contracts_for_its_gaps (integration.rs): the advice with nothing solved; new ArrayList<>(n) is the violation capacity(n=-1) the interpreter reproduces with the JVM's message, Verified with the exception declared (1 tested), a contract that says it never throws is refuted by the JVM and goes back to the agent, assume: capacity >= 0 meets the gap; Random nextBytes/nextInt contracts give a violation the JVM runs, two proofs, and a witness the JVM does not reproduce; StringBuilder.append result == this; a monitor next to the call is refused; the auto fallback and a regression proof. The 4c part one test now gets the violations the JVM gives on 1b's reproducers under advised, from the contract library. All Rust tests pass (141 unit, 5 conformance, 60 integration, 1 skill), the native regression test the_tools_own_checker_agrees_with_jbmc_on_integer_proofs after a rerun (it failed once at 629 s on a loaded machine, and passed alone in 18 s); 158 Python tests pass. Re-rendering every page changed none, and no job was needed, since no recorded example runs JBMC under advised. Not done: --confirm still does not ask JBMC about a proof that rests on contracts. Phase 4 is done apart from removing the text parser, which waits on job 20261106-073804.

commits.summary: The benchmark corpus: the conformance corpus, four documented bugs with their broken and fixed versions, and twelve held-out regressions, run on both engines under strict, assume and advised, with every expected answer and every witness checked on the JVM and correctness, coverage, time and memory kept apart (verification pending)
commits.body:
Step 5a of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. lib/benchmark/ holds 118 cases in the brief's three groups. Group 1 is the conformance corpus's 93 claims, written to conformance.json by a new test in lib/tests/conformance.rs that fails when the file is not the corpus. Group 2 is four documented bugs, each with its broken and fixed version as a source tree: JDK-5045582's binarySearch midpoint, FindBugs' RV_ABSOLUTE_VALUE_OF_HASHCODE, Java Puzzlers' Oddity, and CERT NUM00-J's overflowing range check. Each bug has three cases, the ecosystem review's sequence: the broken property refuted, the fixed one proved, and a regression proof that the fix changes only what it meant to. A fourth case for JDK-5045582 is the whole search, which agrees on every array of up to 8 elements: a real bug outside the proof's domain. Group 3 is twelve regressions written after the engines' optimizations, over the workloads step 5b tabulates (scalar arithmetic, div/rem, binary search, UTF-8 length, array mutation, records), three of them violations.

The expected answers come from the JVM, not the tool. Reference.java states each claim of groups 2 and 3 in Java, apart from the tool's harness generator and expression language, and runs each version in its own class loader. A violation case's witness must refute the claim there. A verified case is searched on boundary values and 200,000 seeded inputs, which is evidence, not proof. lib/benchmark/run.py runs each case on --engine native and --engine jbmc under --gaps strict, assume and advised (the contract library, --max-trust 0) with matched settings: one harness, unwind 16, arrays of up to 8, a 120 s deadline. It classifies each run as correct, correct assuming a named gap, unsupported with its reason, false success, or false alarm. It runs every reported witness on the JVM, and records wall and CPU seconds, peak memory from wait4 (which counts JBMC: a 300 MB grandchild reads as 308 MB) and the solver's figures. It writes results.json and RESULTS.md.

Verified: the 14 tests of lib/benchmark/test_run.py pass (classification, matched commands, witness arguments, measurement, the tables, and Reference.java listing exactly the corpus's ids). Unit (140), conformance (6) and skill tests pass; the integration suite was not run, since the only change to lib/src is help text. Inline, the own checker alone over groups 2 and 3 at a 20 s deadline: the JVM bears out all 25 answers, and 24 of 25 cases are correct in each mode, with none wrong, a median of 0.1 s and 73 MB at most. real/bucket/fix-confined (Math.abs(hash) % b against (hash & 0x7fffffff) % b for non-negative hashes) runs out of time, as it did past 100 s under the default deadline: a held-out finding about the lazy division. A five-run smoke test of the JBMC side found nothing unexpected.

Verification pending: job 20261106-094317-benchmark-corpus-step-5a-both-engines-un (verification/jobs/), the full run of about 700 runs, which writes lib/benchmark/RESULTS.md and results.json. Also fixed: lib/README.md still said --gaps advised needs --engine native or auto, which step 4c's second part made untrue, and the --engine help said the own checker has no arrays. The brief is not wrong, but this step departs from it three ways, recorded under Progress: there is no CVE kernel; group 2's properties are stated from their published sources and held to the JVM, not reviewed by a person; and group 3 is held out from the optimizations' development but not from their author, this session.

commits.summary: Per-phase measurements for both engines: every checker run split into loading, lowering, symbolic execution, encoding, solving and trace, with its formula's size, JBMC's read from its own timings and message times, and a table per workload of which phase dominates (verification pending)

Step 5b of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. lib/src/phases.rs gives each checker run a Profile, the same phases for the tool's own checker and JBMC, recorded on search.runs as phases and formula. The own checker extends bmc::Stats with loading, decoding, encoding and witness seconds; symbolic execution is what the others leave of the run. JBMC now runs under --json-ui --timestamp monotonic. Its Runtime lines give symbolic execution, encoding (Convert SSA, Post-process) and solving, and the times of its messages give loading, lowering and the trace. A run cut off by its deadline or memory gives the rest of its time to the phase it was in. Each run's formula records JBMC's SSA steps and verification conditions, and the variables and clauses. The drivers time their own steps in search.phases: setup, harness, gap scans and preflights, contracts, replay, and the JVM witness run.

Found on the way: a clock read costs about 0.3 us on this WSL2 ARM machine (574 ns per timed region). Timing every word-level circuit operation cost as much as the encoding it measured (example 142: 7.14 s to 7.38 s, against 0.24 s of encoding). The own checker now times a random 1 in 64 operations, takes off the clock's own measured cost, and scales up.

lib/benchmark/run.py carries each run's phases (the checker's own, JBMC's start and output, the driver's steps, the rest of the process) and its largest formula into results.json. RESULTS.md gains 'Where the time goes, by workload, under strict', a row per workload and engine with each phase's share and the dominant one. Group 4 adds the recorded examples the brief names, 141 (binary search) and 142 (UTF-8), patched onto Mica and run under strict, with a table of their own. jbmc-patch-queue.md gains an evidence section that maps each candidate patch to the phase it would shrink, with the first inline figures. On the bounded binarySearch JBMC took 45 s, 94% of it solving 3.28 million clauses, against the own checker's 3.1 s and 240,000 clauses. That points at the formula's size, not arithmetic, for that workload. The ranking itself waits for the job.

Verified: all Rust tests (145 unit, among them the phase readers on CBMC-shaped fixtures, a cut-off run in each phase and the sampled encoding estimate; 6 conformance; 60 integration on the real JBMC 6.11.0; 1 skill), 17 runner tests, and 159 build.py tests, one of them new for the schema's phases and formula. Every recorded result still validates against the schema. Inline, the own checker over groups 2-4 at a 20 s deadline was correct on every case but real/bucket/fix-confined, out of time as in 5a, with solving dominant wherever a run takes more than a fraction of a second (141 at 89%, 142 at 92%). One inline JBMC run, the bounded binarySearch, reached 1.4 GB, past CLAUDE.md's 1 GB guideline for inline work. The full run is job 20261106-102624-benchmark-corpus-with-per-phase-measurem. It supersedes 20261106-094317, which runs the same cases at the 5a revision without phases.

The brief departs in three ways, recorded under Progress. The own checker has no separate encoding pass: it builds the formula as it explores, so encoding is the time inside its circuit builders. Peak memory is per process, not per phase. And ranking the patch candidates waits for the job's table.
